topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove the Monotone Convergence Theorem. Let $s_1 = 1$ and $s_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2}(s_n + \frac{a}{s_n})$ for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, where $a > 0$. Prove that $(s_n)$ converges to $\sqrt{a}$.
concept_tested: Monotone Convergence Theorem and Heron's Algorithm for $\sqrt{a}$
approach: Prove the general MCT for bounded increasing sequences. Then show $s_n^2 \ge a$ for $n \ge 2$, $(s_n)$ is decreasing for $n \ge 2$ and bounded below, apply MCT, and find $L = \sqrt{a}$.

solution_steps.title: Statement of Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: \text{A monotone sequence of real numbers is convergent } \iff \text{it is bounded.} \quad \text{If bounded increasing, } \lim x_n = \sup\{x_n\}; \text{ if bounded decreasing, } \lim x_n = \inf\{x_n\}.
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence that is both monotone and bounded always converges to its supremum (if increasing) or infimum (if decreasing).

solution_steps.title: Proof of Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: S = \{x_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \ne \emptyset, \, S \text{ bounded above} \implies x = \sup S \in \mathbb{R}. \quad \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } x - \epsilon < x_K \le x. \quad n \ge K \implies x - \epsilon < x_K \le x_n \le x < x + \epsilon \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Axiom of $\mathbb{R}$, $S$ has a supremum $x$. Since $x - \epsilon$ is not an upper bound, some $x_K > x - \epsilon$. Since $(x_n)$ is increasing, $x_n \ge x_K > x - \epsilon$ for all $n \ge K$, while $x_n \le x < x + \epsilon$. Thus $|x_n - x| < \epsilon$, proving $\lim x_n = \sup S$.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Boundedness of $(s_n)$ for $n \ge 2$
solution_steps.math: s_{n+1}^2 - a = \frac{1}{4}\left(s_n + \frac{a}{s_n}\right)^2 - a = \frac{1}{4}\left(s_n - \frac{a}{s_n}\right)^2 \ge 0 \implies s_{n+1} \ge \sqrt{a} \quad (\forall n \ge 1)
solution_steps.explanation: Completing the square proves $s_n \ge \sqrt{a} > 0$ for all $n \ge 2$, so the sequence is bounded below by $\sqrt{a}$.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity of $(s_n)$ for $n \ge 2$
solution_steps.math: s_n - s_{n+1} = s_n - \frac{1}{2}\left(s_n + \frac{a}{s_n}\right) = \frac{s_n^2 - a}{2s_n} \ge 0 \quad (\forall n \ge 2) \implies s_{n+1} \le s_n
solution_steps.explanation: Since $s_n^2 \ge a$ and $s_n > 0$ for $n \ge 2$, the difference is non-negative, proving $(s_n)_{n=2}^\infty$ is monotonically decreasing.

solution_steps.title: Apply MCT and Solve for Limit
solution_steps.math: (s_n)_{n=2}^\infty \text{ bounded below and decreasing} \implies L = \lim s_n \text{ exists with } L \ge \sqrt{a}. \quad L = \frac{1}{2}\left(L + \frac{a}{L}\right) \implies 2L^2 = L^2 + a \implies L = \sqrt{a}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, $(s_n)$ converges to a real limit $L \ge \sqrt{a} > 0$. Taking limits on both sides of the recurrence equation gives $L = \sqrt{a}$.

final_answer: By the Monotone Convergence Theorem, $(s_n)$ converges to $L = \sqrt{a}$.
exam_tip: Notice that $s_1 = 1$ may not be $\ge \sqrt{a}$; monotonicity begins at $n = 2$.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Prove that every contractive sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ is a Cauchy sequence. Let $f_1=1, f_2=1$ and $f_{n+1}=f_n+f_{n-1}$. Define $x_n = \frac{f_n}{f_{n+1}}$. Prove that $\lim x_n = \frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
concept_tested: Contractive Sequences, Cauchy Property, and Fibonacci Ratio Limit
approach: Prove contractive implies Cauchy via geometric series bound. Then show $x_{n+1} = 1/(1 + x_n)$ and solve $L = 1/(1+L)$ for golden ratio conjugate.

solution_steps.title: Part 1: Contractive $\implies$ Cauchy
solution_steps.explanation: By repeated application of the contractive definition.

solution_steps.title: Telescoping Sum and Bound for $m > n$
solution_steps.explanation: Since $0 < C < 1$, $C^{n-1} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$. For any $\epsilon > 0$, choosing $H$ large enough makes this bound $< \epsilon$. Thus $(x_n)$ is Cauchy.

solution_steps.title: Part 2: Fibonacci Ratio Recurrence
solution_steps.explanation: Express $x_n$ in terms of $x_{n-1}$.

solution_steps.title: Convergence and Evaluation of Limit
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1/2 \le x_n \le 1$ for all $n \ge 1$, $C = 4/9 < 1$, so $(x_n)$ is contractive and converges to $L$.

solution_steps.title: Calculate Value of Limit
solution_steps.math: L = \frac{1}{1 + L} \implies L^2 + L - 1 = 0 \implies L = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{1 + 4}}{2} = \frac{-1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $x_n > 0$, we take the positive root $L = \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} = \frac{1}{\phi}$.

final_answer: Every contractive sequence is Cauchy and hence convergent in $\mathbb{R}$. The Fibonacci ratio sequence converges to $L = \frac{-1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
exam_tip: Note that $L = (\sqrt{5}-1)/2 = 1/\phi \approx 0.6180339$, the reciprocal of the golden ratio.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove the Nested Intervals Property of real numbers.
approach: State the theorem for closed bounded nested intervals, prove non-empty intersection, and prove uniqueness when length converges to 0.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: I_n = [a_n, b_n], \quad I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N} \implies \exists \xi \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } \xi \in I_n \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Furthermore, if $\inf\{b_n - a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = 0$, then the common point $\xi$ is unique.

solution_steps.title: Monotonicity of Endpoints
solution_steps.math: a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots \le a_n \le \dots \le b_m \le \dots \le b_2 \le b_1 \quad (\forall n, m \in \mathbb{N})
solution_steps.explanation: Since $I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n$, $[a_{n+1}, b_{n+1}] \subseteq [a_n, b_n]$, so $a_n \le a_{n+1}$ and $b_{n+1} \le b_n$. Moreover, for any $n, m$, $a_n \le a_{\max(n,m)} \le b_{\max(n,m)} \le b_m$.

solution_steps.title: Completeness Axiom Application
solution_steps.math: S = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} \ne \emptyset, \, S \text{ bounded above by } b_1 \implies \xi = \sup S \in \mathbb{R} \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Proof that $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$
solution_steps.math: a_n \le \xi \; (\forall n) \quad \text{and} \quad \xi \le b_n \; (\forall n) \implies a_n \le \xi \le b_n \iff \xi \in [a_n, b_n] = I_n
solution_steps.explanation: Because $\xi = \sup S$, $a_n \le \xi$. Because each $b_n$ is an upper bound of $S$, $\xi \le b_n$.

solution_steps.title: Uniqueness under $\lim(b_n - a_n) = 0$
solution_steps.math: \xi_1, \xi_2 \in \bigcap I_n \implies a_n \le \xi_1, \xi_2 \le b_n \implies 0 \le |\xi_1 - \xi_2| \le b_n - a_n \to 0 \implies \xi_1 = \xi_2
solution_steps.explanation: If the lengths tend to 0, the intersection contains precisely one point.

exam_tip: Give a counterexample to show why closedness is essential: for open intervals $J_n = (0, 1/n)$, $\bigcap J_n = \emptyset$.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: Let $X = (x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers that converges to $x$ and suppose that $x_n \ge 0$ for all $n$. Prove that the sequence $(\sqrt{x_n})$ of positive square roots converges to $\sqrt{x}$.
concept_tested: Continuity of Square Root / Limit of $(\sqrt{x_n})$
approach: Consider cases $x = 0$ and $x > 0$. For $x > 0$, rationalize numerator using $\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x} = \frac{x_n - x}{\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}}$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x = 0$
solution_steps.math: \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = 0, \, x_n \ge 0. \quad \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n \ge K \implies 0 \le x_n < \epsilon^2
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\epsilon^2 > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1 Conclusion
solution_steps.math: 0 \le x_n < \epsilon^2 \implies 0 \le \sqrt{x_n} < \epsilon \implies |\sqrt{x_n} - 0| < \epsilon \; (\forall n \ge K)
solution_steps.explanation: Taking square roots preserves order for non-negative numbers, so $\lim \sqrt{x_n} = 0 = \sqrt{0}$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: $x > 0$ — Rationalizing the Difference
solution_steps.math: |\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x}| = \left|\frac{(\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x})(\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x})}{\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}}\right| = \frac{|x_n - x|}{\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}}
solution_steps.explanation: Multiply and divide by conjugate $\sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x}$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: Bounding the Denominator
solution_steps.math: \sqrt{x_n} \ge 0 \implies \sqrt{x_n} + \sqrt{x} \ge \sqrt{x} \implies |\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x}| \le \frac{|x_n - x|}{\sqrt{x}}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{x_n} \ge 0$, the denominator is at least $\sqrt{x} > 0$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists K : n \ge K \implies |x_n - x| < \epsilon\sqrt{x} \implies |\sqrt{x_n} - \sqrt{x}| < \frac{\epsilon\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}} = \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $\lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt{x_n} = \sqrt{x}$.

exam_tip: Do NOT forget to treat $x = 0$ separately, because dividing by $\sqrt{x}$ is undefined when $x = 0$!

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove Cauchy's criterion for uniform convergence of sequences of functions.
concept_tested: Cauchy Criterion for Uniform Convergence of Sequences of Functions
approach: Prove both directions: $f_n \rightrightarrows f \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists H, \forall n, m \ge H, \forall x \in A, |f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: (f_n) \text{ converges uniformly on } A \iff \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists H \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } \forall n, m \ge H, \; \sup_{x \in A} |f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: A sequence of functions converges uniformly if and only if it satisfies the uniform Cauchy criterion.

solution_steps.title: Forward Direction ($\implies$)
solution_steps.math: f_n \rightrightarrows f \implies \exists H : n \ge H \implies |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} \; (\forall x \in A)
solution_steps.explanation: For $n, m \ge H$: $|f_n(x) - f_m(x)| \le |f_n(x) - f(x)| + |f(x) - f_m(x)| < \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} = \epsilon$ for all $x \in A$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction ($\impliedby$): Pointwise Limit
solution_steps.math: \forall x_0 \in A, \; |f_n(x_0) - f_m(x_0)| < \epsilon \implies (f_n(x_0)) \text{ is Cauchy in } \mathbb{R} \implies f(x_0) = \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n(x_0) \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By Cauchy completeness of $\mathbb{R}$, $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to some limit function $f: A \to \mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Backward Direction: Uniformity of the Limit
solution_steps.math: n, m \ge H \implies |f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \epsilon. \quad \text{Take } m \to \infty: \quad |f_n(x) - f(x)| \le \epsilon \quad \forall n \ge H, \; \forall x \in A
solution_steps.explanation: Passing to the limit as $m \to \infty$ with $n \ge H$ fixed preserves the weak inequality $\le \epsilon < 2\epsilon$, establishing uniform convergence.

final_answer: $(f_n)$ converges uniformly on $A$ if and only if it satisfies the Cauchy criterion on $A$.
exam_tip: The power of this criterion is that it establishes uniform convergence WITHOUT needing to know the limit function $f$ in advance.

topic: Topic 3: Sequences of Real Numbers, Convergence & Cauchy Sequences
question: State and prove the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem for sequences of real numbers.
approach: State the theorem and prove using the Monotone Subsequence Theorem + Monotone Convergence Theorem, or by bisection of intervals.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \text{Every bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.}
solution_steps.explanation: If $(x_n)$ is bounded, there exists a subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ that converges in $\mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Existence of Monotonic Subsequence (Peak Points)
solution_steps.math: x_m \text{ is a peak if } x_m \ge x_n \; \forall n \ge m. \quad \text{Case 1: } \infty \text{ peaks } \implies x_{m_1} \ge x_{m_2} \ge \dots \text{ (decreasing)}. \quad \text{Case 2: finitely many peaks } \implies \text{chase strictly larger elements (increasing)}.
solution_steps.explanation: By the Monotone Subsequence Theorem, every sequence has a monotonic subsequence: either infinitely many peak points exist (producing a decreasing subsequence), or past the last peak every term is exceeded by a later term (producing a strictly increasing subsequence).

solution_steps.title: Step 2: Subsequence Inherits Boundedness
solution_steps.math: (x_n) \text{ is bounded} \implies \exists M > 0 \text{ s.t. } -M \le x_n \le M \; (\forall n) \implies -M \le x_{n_k} \le M \; (\forall k)
solution_steps.explanation: Since $(x_{n_k})$ is a subsequence of $(x_n)$, every term $x_{n_k}$ satisfies the same bounds.

solution_steps.title: Step 3: Application of Monotone Convergence Theorem
solution_steps.math: (x_{n_k}) \text{ is bounded and monotone} \implies (x_{n_k}) \text{ converges to a real limit } x^*
solution_steps.explanation: If $(x_{n_k})$ is increasing, $x^* = \sup\{x_{n_k}\}$; if decreasing, $x^* = \inf\{x_{n_k}\}$.

final_answer: Every bounded sequence in $\mathbb{R}$ contains a convergent subsequence.
exam_tip: The two-step proof (Monotone Subsequence Theorem + Monotone Convergence Theorem) is the cleanest and fastest method in Bartle & Sherbert.
